title: How To Shorten Your Work Day
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin explains how deliberately shortening the workday, rather than working late to feel productive, actually improves efficiency, creativity, and clarity of thought, citing his own 31-year practice of leaving school at a fixed time regardless of unfinished tasks. He grounds the strategy in Parkinson's Law, the principle that a task expands to fill the time allotted for its completion, meaning a shorter, non-negotiable deadline forces sharper prioritization and less wasted effort. Referencing Jocko Willink's idea that discipline equals freedom, he frames the fixed departure time as a form of self-imposed constraint that ultimately produces more usable time outside of school, not less accomplished at school. The article recommends starting with a moderately challenging fixed departure time and gradually shrinking it further as it becomes easy, rather than attempting a drastic cut immediately. It closes by promising that the resulting improvement isn't a rushed, scattered experience but genuinely sharper and calmer work.
points: Deliberately shortening the workday with a fixed, non-negotiable departure time, rather than lingering to feel productive, improves efficiency and clarity of thought.

A fixed constraint on time is described as a form of self-imposed discipline that ultimately creates more usable time outside of school.
The recommended approach is to start with a moderately challenging departure time and gradually shrink it further once it stops being a challenge.
The resulting efficiency is described as calmer and smarter, not a rushed or scatter-brained experience.
quotes: Efficiency has been a priority for me for the past 31 years of teaching. It’s a big reason why I continue to teach, with zero plans to retire.
Former Navy Seal and author Jocko Willink has a book called Discipline Equals Freedom , and I think it’s absolutely true. To make room for life outside of school, you must have discipline.
Parkinson’s Law is the tendency for organizations and individuals to expand a task in complexity and importance in relation to the time given for its completion.
I recommend getting started by creating a firm time for leaving school that moderately challenges you to get your work done. When that no longer becomes a challenge, shrink the deadline.
You’re not moving faster per se, you’re getting smarter and more discerning, which translates to speed. You may even find yourself physically slowing down and becoming calmer .
